BUCSS: Bias and Uncertainty Corrected Sample Size

Source: R/BUCSS.R
BUCSS-package.Rd

Implements sample size planning for a future study from the summary statistics of a prior study, correcting the prior effect for publication bias and uncertainty so the planned study attains its target statistical power more reliably than methods that take a sample effect size at face value. The correction builds on the truncated noncentral distribution of Taylor and Muller (1996) and is described in Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017).

Details

Each ss_buc_* function plans one analysis. The t tests: ss_buc_one_sample_t, ss_buc_paired_t, ss_buc_independent_t, and ss_buc_welch_t. Between-subjects analysis of variance and covariance: ss_buc_one_way_anova, ss_buc_factorial_anova, ss_buc_factorial_anova_general, and ss_buc_ancova. Within-subjects and split-plot analysis of variance: ss_buc_rm_anova, ss_buc_rm_anova_general, ss_buc_mixed_anova, and ss_buc_mixed_anova_general. Regression and correlation: ss_buc_reg_coef, ss_buc_R2, ss_buc_reg_joint, and ss_buc_correlation. And ss_buc_manova for a two-group multivariate comparison and ss_buc_chisq_diff for the chi square difference between nested models. The experimental designs among these, their tests, and the statistical power of those tests are described in Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027). ss_buc_sensitivity simulates the literature a plan came from and reports how often such a plan attains its target power, and plot draws the largest assurance a prior result can support.

The planners carried over from BUCSS 1.x are also available, through a web interface, as Shiny apps at https://designingexperiments.com; the designs added in 2.0.0 are available in R only.

BUCSS follows the design and naming conventions of the DMAR package (Design, Measurement, and Analysis in R): its ss_buc_* planners parallel the ss_aipe_* (accuracy in parameter estimation) and ss_power_* (power analysis) sample size planning families in DMAR, returning a tidy result object in the same house style. DMAR is a natural companion for effect size estimation, confidence intervals, and sample size planning across additional frameworks.

The bias and uncertainty adjusted noncentrality parameter is found by solving the truncated-likelihood equation directly with uniroot, so it is no longer capped at 100 (the 1.x grid bound) and needs no resolution argument.

How assurance is used. Every planner takes an assurance: the long run proportion of planned studies whose power at the true effect reaches or surpasses the desired power, when each is planned from a prior study published under the rule alpha_prior describes. A planned study reaches its target power whenever the noncentrality parameter it was planned from is at or below the true one, because power rises with the effect (and, apart from rounding the sample size up to a whole number and from the smallest sample size a planner returns, the design's own minimum or the Welch planner's 10 per group, only then). The planners therefore plan from the lower limit of a one-sided confidence interval for the prior study's noncentrality parameter, at confidence level assurance, computed from the distribution of the prior statistic truncated at the publication threshold: the value at which a published prior study would exceed the observed statistic with probability 1 - assurance (what Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell, 2017, call the (1 - assurance) quantile of the likelihood distribution). At assurance = .5 this is the median unbiased estimate, which corrects for publication bias only; above .5 it adds the correction for uncertainty. The term follows Kelley and Maxwell (2003), who used assurance in sample size planning for the probability that a confidence interval will be no wider than desired; here it is the probability that the planned study's power will be at least the desired power. ss_buc_sensitivity checks the proportion by simulation for any plan, counting a refusal to plan as meeting the target, as the guarantee does, and also reporting the rate among the plans issued.

The planning effect size. Every plan also reports a planning effect size, in a row whose name ends in _planning (smd_planning, f_planning, rho_planning, and so on). It is an adjusted effect size: the value, in the design's usual effect size metric, used to plan the sample size given the situation at hand (the prior study's result, the publication bias assumed through alpha_prior, and the uncertainty allowed for through assurance). It is ncp_adjusted restated in that metric and is what the plan is built on, not an estimate of the population effect to report: above an assurance of .5 it is deliberately conservative (a lower confidence limit), and at .5 it is the median unbiased estimate. Each planner's Value section names its metric.

Safeguard power is a special case. Safeguard power (Perugini, Gallucci, & Costantini, 2014) is a way of planning a new study from a prior study's effect size that guards against the prior estimate being too large. Instead of planning for the effect size the prior study observed, the researcher plans for the lower limit of a two-sided 60 percent confidence interval around it (a limit that, in repeated sampling, falls below the true effect 80 percent of the time), so the new study keeps its intended power even if the true effect is somewhat smaller than the one observed. It allows for uncertainty in the prior estimate but not for publication bias.

It is the special case alpha_prior = 1 and assurance = .80 of the method here, that is, BUCSS without the publication bias correction, at an assurance of .80. alpha_prior is the significance level a prior result had to reach to be published, and no p value exceeds 1, so alpha_prior = 1, which may also be written alpha_prior = "No Publication Filter", means no publication filter: any result would have been published, the truncation is removed, and the prior statistic has its ordinary distribution. (Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell, 2017, p. 1552, note that this level can be set equal to 1 when publication bias is thought not to apply.) At assurance = .80 the adjusted noncentrality parameter is then the lower limit of a one-sided 80 percent confidence interval, which is the lower limit of the two-sided 60 percent interval (either way, 20 percent lies below it), and the plan is the smallest sample size whose ordinary power at that value reaches desired_power. In general, the lower limit of a two-sided interval at confidence level C is assurance = (1 + C)/2, so a two-sided 80 percent interval is assurance = .90.

For an F or chi square statistic the correspondence is exact: the adjusted noncentrality parameter is the lower limit of that interval, computed from the statistic's ordinary noncentral distribution. Two differences from safeguard power remain, and each can only make the plan here the same as the safeguard plan or larger. First, for the t tests and every other effect on one degree of freedom, safeguard power computes its interval from the signed t, while the interval here bounds the size of the effect whatever its sign, because the publication rule is two-sided. That difference is negligible for a convincing prior result and grows as the prior result weakens. Second, an unbalanced prior design is read as a balanced one, and the Welch planner returns at least 10 per group. vignette("understanding-assurance", package = "BUCSS") measures both. For the regression planners the equivalence holds in the frame random_predictors names. With alpha_prior below 1 the same construction is applied to the publication-truncated distribution, which is what the bias correction adds to safeguard power.

Anderson, S. F., Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2017). Sample-size planning for more accurate statistical power: A method adjusting sample effect sizes for publication bias and uncertainty. Psychological Science, 28, 1547–1562. doi:10.1177/0956797617723724

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8, 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

Perugini, M., Gallucci, M., & Costantini, G. (2014). Safeguard power as a protection against imprecise power estimates. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 9, 319–332. doi:10.1177/1745691614528519
